input: Compressing a gas in a single stage is, among other things, an exercise in watching temperature follow pressure upward. Consider a single-stage compressor handling natural gas, which it raises from 2 bar to 9 bar. The gas arrives at an inlet temperature of 293 K, and for the isentropic compression of that gas, with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature works out at 450 K. That figure deserves a moment of attention, because it is an idealised one. The isentropic estimate is built on a compression with no mechanical losses, and a real machine is never quite so tidy: friction and the other imperfections of actual hardware add their share of heat to the gas as it passes through. It is for precisely this reason that the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than the estimate. The estimate should therefore be read as the tidy limiting case against which the messier reality of the installed compressor is compared, and the gap between the two is, in effect, the thermal signature of everything the idealisation left out. None of this makes the estimate useless; it makes it a baseline, valuable exactly because it states what the compression alone would produce before the machinery adds its own contribution. Used in that spirit, the figure earns its keep: it tells the engineer what the compression itself demands, cleanly separated from what the hardware happens to add, and any discussion of the machine's condition can then begin from the size of the gap rather than from the raw discharge reading alone. That separation is the real service the idealised number performs.
target: A single-stage compressor raises natural gas from 2 bar to 9 bar, and the discharge temperature under isentropic compression is the quantity calculated here. The inlet temperature is 293 K and the heat-capacity ratio is 1.4. The isentropic estimate gives a discharge temperature of 450 K. Compression work raises the gas temperature as the pressure rises; the size of the rise is set by the pressure change and the heat-capacity ratio, and no other property of the gas enters the estimate. The estimate is limited to isentropic compression. Mechanical losses are not included in it, and the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than the estimate. The difference between the measured temperature and the estimate is the part of the heating that the idealised compression does not carry. The estimate is used as the baseline for the installed machine: a measured discharge temperature at the estimate would leave the losses unaccounted for, and a measured temperature below the estimate would contradict the stated exclusion. The result is valid for the stated inlet temperature, pressures, and heat-capacity ratio. The estimate can be read in the other direction as well. A discharge temperature is the temperature the gas must reach when the stated pressure rise is produced with no loss counted; the work put into the gas appears as internal energy, and the temperature is where that work is visible. Intercooling, leakage past the moving parts, and heat exchange with the surroundings are all outside the stated case, and the case does not need them: it fixes the ideal temperature for the stated rise so that the installed machine can be compared against a case with nothing in it but compression. A machine whose measured temperature approaches the estimate is a machine whose losses are small against the work of compression; the comparison, not the estimate alone, carries that information.
